module


public import Mathlib.Algebra.Polynomial.Bivariate
public import Mathlib.RingTheory.Algebraic.Pi

@[expose] public noncomputable section

/-!
# Algebra over the Ring of Polynomials

-/

variable {R S : Type*} [CommSemiring R] [CommSemiring S] [Algebra R S]

namespace Polynomial

instance instAlgebraPi : Algebra R[X] (S → S) :=
  (RingHom.pi fun s ↦ (Polynomial.aeval s).toRingHom).toAlgebra

@[simp]
lemma algebraMap_algebraPi (p : R[X]) (s : S) : algebraMap R[X] (S → S) p s = aeval s p := rfl

@[simp] lemma aeval_polynomial_pi (p : R[X][X]) (f : S → S) (x : S) :
    p.aeval f x = aevalAeval x (f x) p := by
  induction p using Polynomial.induction_on' with
  | add => simp [*]
  | monomial n q =>
  simp only [aeval_monomial, Pi.mul_apply, Pi.pow_apply, aevalAevalEquiv_apply_apply,
    algebraMap_def, coe_mapRingHom, eval_mul, eval_map_algebraMap, eval_pow, eval_C]
  induction q using Polynomial.induction_on' with
  | add => simp [add_mul, *]
  | monomial n p => simp

end Polynomial

findings.description: The evaluation algebra is mathematically valid, but registering it globally at lines 33–34 introduces a genuinely unequal instance diamond with Mathlib's ordinary function-space algebra and scalar action. For R = ℕ and S = ℕ[X], the new inferred algebra satisfies `algebraMap ℕ[X] (ℕ[X] → ℕ[X]) X 0 = 0`, whereas `Function.algebra ℕ[X] ℕ[X]` sends X to the constant function X. Moreover, independently inferred scalar multiplication gives `(X • (1 : ℕ[X] → ℕ[X])) 0 = X`, while `(algebraMap ℕ[X] (ℕ[X] → ℕ[X]) X * 1) 0 = 0`. These inequalities, including inequality of the two Algebra structures, were proved in the scratch file. This is not a contradiction in Lean: the two instance paths select different operations. The inspected complex-function use sites select the intended evaluation algebra and are unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: Mathlib/RingTheory/Algebraic/Pi.lean:33–38 explicitly says the evaluation action is not an instance because it forms a diamond with Pi.instSMul; lines 55–57 give the same warning for Polynomial.algebraPi. Mathlib/Algebra/Algebra/Pi.lean:38–48 and 134–138 define the ordinary pointwise algebra. MathlibTest/InstanceDiamonds.lean:179–191 proves related evaluation-versus-pointwise actions unequal.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep evaluation-algebra selection local or explicitly scoped rather than global. Use `letI := Polynomial.algebraPi R S S` with the canonical identity S-algebra in the intended lemmas and problem statements, as Erdős 229 already does.

findings.description: The construction duplicates the specialization `Polynomial.algebraPi R S S` already supplied by the directly imported Mathlib.RingTheory.Algebraic.Pi module, with the canonical identity Algebra S S. Both have algebra map p ↦ (s ↦ aeval s p) and the same scalar action. Equality of the complete Algebra structures was proved as `Review.same_as_mathlib` in /workspace/review/scratch.lean. This is duplication, not a mathematical mismatch between the evaluation constructions.
findings.source_evidence: Mathlib/RingTheory/Algebraic/Pi.lean:53–68 defines the more general `Polynomial.algebraPi R S T`, whose algebra map is `fun p z => algebraMap S T (aeval z p)`. Specializing T = S with the identity self-algebra gives precisely this file's construction.
findings.suggested_fix: Reuse Mathlib's Polynomial.algebraPi specialization instead of maintaining a second implementation, preferably with the local/scoped selection recommended for the instance-diamond concern.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/513.lean:52–56, the docstring claims that every transcendental entire function has liminf ratio greater than 1/2. The Lean theorem correctly asserts only that the supremum over those functions is greater than 1/2. The universal docstring is false: for f(z) = exp(z), the ratio is `exp(-r) * max_n r^n/n!`, which tends to 0 by Stirling's formula.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/513 defines B as the supremum over transcendental entire functions and says that Kövári observed B > 1/2; it also records Clunie–Hayman's stronger bound 4/7 < B. These are lower bounds on B, not on every individual function's liminf.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to say that the supremum of the liminf ratios over transcendental entire functions exceeds 1/2. Leave the Lean statement unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The source's transcendental entire function is represented using `Transcendental ℂ[X] f` and `Differentiable ℂ f`. The sequence is indexed by all naturals, with the conclusion restricted to n ≥ 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Under the selected evaluation algebra, algebraicity means that a nonzero bivariate polynomial P satisfies P(z,f(z)) = 0 for every z. A polynomial root bound then bounds an entire f by a power of |z| outside a disk; Cauchy estimates force f to be a polynomial. Conversely, a polynomial q satisfies Y − q(X) = 0. Thus transcendence here is exactly being a non-polynomial entire function. The extra sequence entry S 0 is harmless: extend a positively indexed sequence by S 0 = ∅, or discard the zeroth entry.

reformulations.difference: Barth–Schneider's phrase 'transcendental entire function' is represented by algebraic transcendence over ℂ[X] together with complex differentiability everywhere.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The Mathlib evaluation algebra used explicitly here turns IsAlgebraic ℂ[X] f into a nonzero relation P(z,f(z)) ≡ 0. For entire f such a relation implies polynomial growth by a root bound, hence polynomiality by Cauchy estimates. Conversely polynomial functions satisfy Y − q(X) = 0. The positive derivative orders in Lean agree with Theorem 1 of the primary paper.

reformulations.difference: The source uses power-series coefficients and maxima, whereas Lean uses iterated derivatives divided by factorials and suprema; it also expresses transcendental entirety using Transcendental ℂ[X] and Differentiable ℂ.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For an entire function, a_n = f^(n)(0)/n!. For r > 0 the Taylor terms tend to zero, so their nonnegative magnitudes attain their supremum; continuity and compactness give the maximum on the circle. Thus ratio agrees with the source near infinity. Algebraic entire functions over ℂ[X] are precisely polynomial functions: a polynomial relation gives polynomial growth by a root bound, then Cauchy estimates; the converse uses Y − q(X). Hence the supremum ranges over exactly the source's functions.

reformulations.difference: The family of transcendental entire functions is specified through transcendence as elements of the evaluation ℂ[X]-algebra of functions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A nonzero polynomial relation over ℂ[X] is exactly P(z,f(z)) ≡ 0. For an entire f, polynomial root bounds and Cauchy estimates make this equivalent to f being polynomial; conversely every polynomial q has the relation Y − q(X). Therefore the Lean family is the source's family, and its supremum upper bound is the recorded bound B ≤ 2/π − c.

reformulations.difference: The source's class of transcendental entire functions is expressed using algebraic transcendence over ℂ[X]. This equivalence concerns the function class, not the erroneous universal wording of the docstring.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For entire f, a relation P(z,f(z)) ≡ 0 with P nonzero gives polynomial growth and therefore polynomiality by Cauchy estimates. Every polynomial q conversely satisfies Y − q(X) = 0. Thus the supremum in Lean is precisely the source's B, and B > 1/2 is faithfully stated.

reformulations.difference: Lean adopts the source's explicitly intended transcendental version, expressing transcendence over ℂ[X], and omits a separate f ≠ 0 hypothesis.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For entire functions, algebraicity in this evaluation algebra is equivalent to polynomiality: polynomial relations give polynomial growth and Cauchy estimates, while polynomial functions have the relation Y − q(X). Thus the transcendence condition agrees with the source's clarification and already excludes the zero function. Natural-number indexing of a strictly increasing infinite sequence is harmless: if order zero occurs, deleting that first term leaves an allowed infinite tail, whose dense union of zero sets is contained in the original union.

review.notes: All three declarations in the reviewed module were checked; their axiom dependencies contain no sorryAx. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles and proves equality with Mathlib's evaluation algebra, the bivariate algebraicity/transcendence characterizations, the unequal pointwise-algebra witness, and boundary cases for zero/one, ZMod 0, ZMod 1, and polynomial functions over ZMod 2. The finite checks in eval.lean return true. The analytic step 'entire algebraic implies polynomial' was checked mathematically, not proved in Lean, so the full downstream reformulations are marked accordingly. Expression inspection confirms that Erdős 513 and 906 use this instance; Erdős 229 explicitly uses Mathlib.algebraPi instead. No downstream mathematical statement mismatch or stale status was found. Hayman's 1974 full text was blocked and Clunie–Hayman's full text was subscription-only; the exact Erdős source statements and the primary Barth–Schneider theorem were available. No checkout files were edited.
